listeningParts.title: Enrolling a child at a nursery
listeningParts.contextDescription: A father visits a nursery to ask about a place for his daughter.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Hello, you must be Mr Okafor. I'm Sophie, the manager here at Little Acorns. Thanks for coming in.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: Thanks for seeing me. My wife and I are both going back to full-time work in September, so we're looking for a nursery place for our daughter, Ada.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Lovely. How old is Ada?

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: She'll be two in July.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: So she'd join our Squirrels room, which is for children from two to three years old. We have three rooms altogether: Babies, for children up to two, Squirrels, and then Owls, for three- and four-year-olds who are getting ready for school.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: How many children are there in the Squirrels room?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Up to sixteen, with four members of staff, so the ratio is one adult to four children. Each child has a key worker, who's responsible for their care and keeps a record of their development. Parents can see the records and photos through our app.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: That sounds good. What are your opening hours?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We're open from half past seven in the morning until six in the evening, Monday to Friday. We're closed for one week at Christmas and on public holidays, but otherwise we're open all year.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: And the fees?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: A full day is sixty-two pounds. If Ada comes five days a week, there's a five per cent discount. The fee includes all meals and snacks, which are cooked here every day by our chef, and nappies as well. The only extra is if you'd like her to join the weekly music class, which is run by an outside teacher and costs four pounds a session.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: Okay. Ada is a fussy eater, I'm afraid. Is that a problem?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Not at all, it's very common at that age. We never force children to eat, but we encourage them to try new things, and they often eat better when they see their friends eating. We'll let you know every day what she's eaten.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: And does she still need to sleep during the day?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Most children in Squirrels have a nap after lunch, usually for about an hour and a half. We have a quiet room with little beds, and we follow whatever routine you have at home as far as possible.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: What do the children do during the day?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: A lot of it is play, because that's how young children learn best. There's painting, building, sand and water play, stories and songs. We also spend time outside every day, whatever the weather, so please bring a waterproof suit and wellington boots for Ada. And every Friday, the older children go to the woodland area behind the nursery for forest school.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: She'd love that. How does the settling-in work?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We offer three free settling-in sessions before the start date. For the first one, you stay with her for an hour. For the second, you leave her for an hour, and for the third, she stays for a whole morning. That way she gets used to us gradually.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: Great. Is there a place available for September?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Yes, we have two places left in Squirrels. To secure one, we ask for a registration fee of fifty pounds, which isn't refundable, and a deposit of one month's fees, which you get back when she leaves.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: Okay. Can I fill in the form now?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Of course. I'll need Ada's full name and date of birth, and the name of your doctor. Which surgery are you registered with?

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: The Riverside Health Centre.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Perfect, that's just round the corner. And finally, we ask for the names of two people, other than you and your wife, who are allowed to collect Ada. We'll take a photo of them, and we won't let her go with anyone else unless you've told us in advance and given us a password.

dialogue.speaker: Father
dialogue.text: That's reassuring. I'll put down my sister and Ada's grandmother.

listeningParts.title: A new children's discovery centre
listeningParts.contextDescription: A presenter on local radio describes a new science discovery centre for children.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Now, if you're a parent looking for something to do with the kids during the half-term holiday, there's some good news. The new Spark Discovery Centre opens this Saturday in the old tram depot on Canal Street. I went for a preview visit yesterday, and I have to say, I had as much fun as the children did.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: The centre is designed for children aged three to twelve, and the idea is that everything can be touched. There are no glass cases and no signs saying 'Do not touch'. Instead, children learn by experimenting, making mistakes and trying again. The director, Dr Fiona Grant, told me that the aim is to encourage curiosity rather than to teach facts. As she put it, children forget facts, but they remember the feeling of discovering something for themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: The centre is divided into five zones. On the ground floor, the Water Zone is probably the most popular. Children can build dams, control the flow of water using pipes and pumps, and see how boats float. Be warned: they'll get wet, so it's a good idea to bring a change of clothes, although waterproof aprons are provided.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Next to it is the Build Zone, where children can design and construct structures using giant foam blocks, and then test them on an earthquake table that shakes. It's surprisingly difficult to make a tower that survives.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Upstairs, the Body Zone lets children explore how their bodies work. There's a giant model of a heart that you can walk through, and machines that measure how high you can jump or how fast you react. The Light and Sound Zone is in a darkened room, with mirrors, lasers and instruments that make music when you move in front of them.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And finally, for the youngest visitors, there's the Tiny Explorers area, which is reserved for children under five and their parents. It's quieter and softer, with sensory toys and a small sand pit, so toddlers don't get knocked over by the bigger children.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Every day, there are also live science shows in the theatre, at eleven and at three. I saw one about air pressure, which involved a lot of loud bangs and exploding balloons, and the children absolutely loved it.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: One thing I particularly liked is that the centre has thought about children with different needs. On Sunday mornings, from nine until ten, there's a relaxed session for children who find noise and crowds difficult. The lights are lower, the sound effects are turned off, and the number of visitors is kept small. All the exhibits on both floors can be reached by wheelchair, and staff have been trained to help children with disabilities take part fully.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Now, the practical details. The centre is open daily from ten until five, and entry costs nine pounds for children and twelve for adults. Children under two get in free. If you think you'll visit regularly, an annual family membership costs eighty pounds and covers two adults and up to three children, which pays for itself after about two visits. Tickets should be booked online, because numbers are limited to avoid overcrowding.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: There's no car park at the centre, so the organisers recommend using public transport. The number seven bus stops right outside, and the train station is a ten-minute walk away. There's a café on site, but you're also welcome to bring your own food and eat it in the picnic room on the first floor.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Finally, if your children are as excited as mine were, you might be interested in the holiday workshops for eight- to twelve-year-olds. This half term, they're about robotics, and the children build and program a simple robot that they can take home. Places cost twenty-five pounds and are already filling up fast, so book soon if you're interested.

listeningParts.title: Researching bilingual children
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two education students, Mei and Tom, discuss a research project on children who grow up speaking two languages.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: So, Mei, have you finished the literature review for our project on bilingual children?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Almost. I've read about twenty studies, and there are some really interesting findings, but also a lot of disagreement.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Let's start with the basics. When I was growing up, people used to say that learning two languages at once confused children and delayed their speech.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Yes, that was a common belief, especially in the first half of the twentieth century. Some early studies seemed to support it, but they had serious problems. For example, they often tested bilingual children only in their weaker language, or compared poor immigrant children with wealthier monolingual children, so the differences weren't really caused by bilingualism.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: So what does more recent research show?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Bilingual children reach the main milestones, like saying their first words and putting two words together, at about the same age as other children. It's true that if you count their vocabulary in each language separately, it's often smaller than a monolingual child's. But if you add the two languages together, the total is usually the same or even larger.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That makes sense. They might know some words only in one language, depending on where they use them.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Exactly. A child might know kitchen words in the language spoken at home and school words in the other one.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: What about mixing languages? I've noticed my cousin's children do that a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: It's called code-switching, and parents often worry about it, but researchers generally see it as normal and even a sign of skill. Adult bilinguals do it too, and they follow quite complex grammatical rules when they switch.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Okay. Now, the part I'm most interested in is the so-called bilingual advantage. I read that bilingual children are better at concentrating and switching between tasks.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: That's where the disagreement is. In the 2000s, a lot of studies, particularly by Ellen Bialystok in Canada, found that bilingual children performed better on tests of what's called executive function, which includes things like ignoring distractions and switching attention. The theory was that constantly managing two languages exercises these skills.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: And now?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: More recent studies with much larger samples have often found no difference at all. Some researchers think the earlier positive results were partly due to small samples and to publication bias, meaning that studies that found an advantage were more likely to be published.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: So we should present both sides in our report.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Definitely. What's much less controversial is that bilingualism has social and cultural benefits, like being able to communicate with grandparents, and practical advantages later in life, for example in the job market.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Right. Now, for our own small study, we're going to interview parents of bilingual children at the community language school. How many families have agreed to take part?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Twelve so far. I'd hoped for at least fifteen, but some parents were worried about their privacy. I've explained that we won't use any real names.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Good. What should we ask them about?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: I think the most important topic is the strategies they use at home. For example, some families follow the 'one parent, one language' approach, where each parent always speaks a different language to the child. Others speak one language at home and leave the other to school.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: And we should ask about challenges. I imagine a lot of children stop using the home language once they start school, because all their friends speak the majority language.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Yes, that's very common, especially in adolescence. It would be interesting to know what parents do to prevent that.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Okay. Shall I write the interview questions, and you finish the literature review?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Sounds good. Let's meet again on Thursday to check them.

listeningParts.title: How babies learn language
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a developmental psychology course on how infants begin to acquire language.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at one of the most remarkable achievements of early childhood: learning to speak. By the age of five, most children have a vocabulary of several thousand words and can produce complex sentences, without ever having had a formal lesson. How do they do it?

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Surprisingly, language learning begins before birth. From about the twenty-fifth week of pregnancy, a baby can hear sounds from outside the womb, although they're muffled. Experiments have shown that newborn babies prefer their mother's voice to other voices, and that they prefer the language their mother spoke during pregnancy. Researchers discovered this by measuring how fast babies sucked on a special dummy, which tends to increase when they're interested in what they hear. One study even found that the cries of newborn French and German babies have different melodies, which match the patterns of their parents' languages.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the first months of life, babies are what researchers call universal listeners. Every language uses a particular set of sounds, called phonemes, to distinguish words. For example, English distinguishes between 'r' and 'l', but Japanese doesn't. Young babies can hear the difference between almost all the sounds used in the world's languages. But by around ten to twelve months, they gradually lose the ability to distinguish sounds that aren't used in the languages around them. In other words, they become specialists in their own language.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: How do babies work out where one word ends and another begins? In normal speech, there are no pauses between words. One answer comes from a famous study published in 1996 by Jenny Saffran and her colleagues. They played eight-month-old babies a continuous stream of made-up syllables for just two minutes. Within the stream, some syllables always followed each other, forming 'words', while others appeared together only by chance. Afterwards, the babies listened longer to new combinations than to the 'words', showing that they had noticed the patterns. This ability is known as statistical learning.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, babies are practising producing sounds. At around six months, they begin babbling, repeating syllables such as 'ba-ba-ba' or 'da-da-da'. Interestingly, deaf babies who are exposed to sign language babble with their hands, producing repeated movements that resemble signs. This suggests that babbling is not just about controlling the mouth, but a stage in learning language itself.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: First words usually appear at around twelve months, and progress is slow at first. Then, at around eighteen months, many children experience a vocabulary explosion, learning several new words a day. By two, most children are combining words into short phrases, such as 'more milk' or 'daddy gone'.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What role do parents play? Across many cultures, adults speak to babies in a special way, sometimes called infant-directed speech, with a higher pitch, exaggerated intonation and simple words. Studies show babies prefer this kind of speech, and it seems to help them learn. Research by Patricia Kuhl also showed the importance of social interaction. Nine-month-old American babies who played with a Mandarin-speaking adult for twelve sessions learned to distinguish Mandarin sounds. But babies who watched exactly the same sessions on video learned nothing. Real human contact appears to be essential.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, is there a critical period for learning language, after which it becomes much more difficult? Evidence from people learning second languages suggests that those who start in early childhood are much more likely to achieve a native-like accent. Grammar also seems easier to master when learning begins early. However, adults often learn vocabulary faster than children at first, so it's not simply a case of 'younger is better'. In the next lecture, we'll look at the debate about whether humans have an inborn ability for grammar.

readingPassages.title: The children's garden: the invention of kindergarten
paragraphs: Today, it is taken for granted in most countries that young children should spend time in some form of early education before they start school. Yet the idea that children under the age of six could benefit from organised learning is relatively recent. One of the most important figures in its development was a German teacher named Friedrich Froebel, who opened the first kindergarten in 1837 and gave the institution its name, which means 'children's garden'.

Froebel was born in 1782 in a small village in Thuringia, in central Germany. His mother died when he was a baby, and he later described his childhood as lonely and unhappy. He spent much of his time alone in the countryside, developing a deep love of nature that would influence all his later work. As a young man, he studied a range of subjects, including mathematics, architecture and mineralogy, before discovering his talent for teaching while working at a school in Frankfurt. He later said that he had felt from his first lesson as though he had at last found his true calling, and that he never seriously considered any other career afterwards.

At the time, most schools relied heavily on memorisation and strict discipline. Children were expected to sit still, repeat what the teacher said and learn by heart. Froebel was strongly influenced by the Swiss educator Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi, with whom he worked for two years, and who believed that education should develop the whole child, including the hands and the heart as well as the head. Froebel went further, arguing that young children learn best through play, which he described as the highest expression of human development in childhood.

To put his ideas into practice, Froebel designed a series of educational toys, which he called 'gifts'. The first gift was a set of six soft woollen balls in different colours. Later gifts included wooden cubes, cylinders and blocks that could be combined to build shapes and patterns. Through playing with these objects, children were meant to discover basic ideas of form, number and balance for themselves. He also developed 'occupations', such as paper folding, weaving, sewing and modelling with clay, as well as songs and movement games.

Gardens were central to Froebel's vision. In his kindergartens, each child had a small plot of land to look after, as well as a shared garden for the whole group. He believed that caring for plants would teach children patience and responsibility, and help them understand the natural world. The name kindergarten reflected his belief that children, like plants, need the right conditions in order to grow, and that the teacher's role was rather like that of a gardener, providing care and support rather than forcing development.

Froebel's ideas were controversial in his own lifetime. In 1851, the Prussian government banned kindergartens, apparently because officials confused Froebel with his nephew, Karl Froebel, who had written books with radical political and religious views. The ban lasted until 1860, by which time Froebel had died. Ironically, the ban helped to spread his ideas abroad, as many of his followers, a large number of them women, left Germany and opened kindergartens in other countries.

One of these followers, Margarethe Schurz, opened the first kindergarten in the United States in 1856, in Watertown, Wisconsin. It was taught in German, for the children of German immigrants. The first English-language kindergarten in the country was opened in Boston in 1860 by Elizabeth Peabody, who became one of the movement's most energetic supporters. By the end of the nineteenth century, kindergartens had been established in cities across Europe, North America and Japan, and in many places they became part of the public school system. Training colleges for kindergarten teachers were also set up, and for many women at the time, teaching young children offered one of the few respectable careers available to them outside the home.

Froebel's influence can be seen far beyond the kindergarten. Several important architects, including Frank Lloyd Wright, said that playing with Froebel's blocks as a child had shaped their understanding of space and form. More importantly, many of his core beliefs, that young children learn through play and activity, that education should develop the whole child, and that teachers should guide rather than dictate, are now central to early childhood education around the world, even where his name is no longer known.

readingPassages.title: The marshmallow test revisited
paragraphs: In the late 1960s, the psychologist Walter Mischel began a series of experiments at a nursery school at Stanford University in California that would become some of the most famous in the history of psychology. Children aged between three and five were taken into a room and offered a treat, often a marshmallow. They were told that they could eat it immediately, or, if they waited until the researcher returned, they would receive two treats instead. The researcher then left the room for up to fifteen minutes, and the children were observed through a one-way mirror.

The children's responses varied widely. Some ate the marshmallow as soon as the door closed. Others tried to resist but gave in after a few minutes. Around a third managed to wait the full time and received the second treat. Mischel and his colleagues were particularly interested in the strategies the successful children used. Many covered their eyes, turned away from the table, sang to themselves or kicked the desk. Some invented games. The children who did least well tended to stare at the marshmallow, touch it or even smell it.

The experiment might have remained a minor study of self-control had it not been for a coincidence. Mischel's own daughters attended the same nursery school, and as they grew older, he began to ask them casually how their former classmates were getting on. He noticed what seemed to be a pattern: the children who had waited longest appeared to be doing better at school. This led him to contact the original participants years later, when they were teenagers, and to collect information about their academic achievement and behaviour.

The follow-up studies, published in the late 1980s and 1990, produced striking results. Children who had waited longer as preschoolers were described by their parents as more competent and better able to cope with stress as adolescents, and they had higher scores on the SAT, the test used for university admission in the United States. Later studies even suggested that they had healthier body weights as adults. The findings were widely reported, and the marshmallow test became a symbol of the idea that self-control in early childhood can predict success in life.

This idea had a powerful influence on education. Schools and parenting books promoted programmes designed to teach young children to delay gratification, on the assumption that improving self-control would lead to better outcomes later. The message often given to the public was simple: if you can teach your child to resist the marshmallow, you are setting them up for success.

However, in 2018, a team led by Tyler Watts at New York University published a study that challenged this interpretation. They repeated the experiment with more than nine hundred children, a much larger and more varied group than Mischel's, whose original participants had mostly been the children of Stanford University staff. Watts and his colleagues found that the link between waiting time and later achievement was only about half as strong as in the original studies. More importantly, once they took into account factors such as the family's income and the mother's level of education, the link almost disappeared.

This suggests that the ability to wait may be, at least partly, a reflection of children's circumstances rather than a fixed personal quality. Other research supports this view. In a 2012 study at the University of Rochester, children were first promised better art materials by a researcher. In one group, the researcher kept the promise; in the other, he did not. When the marshmallow test followed, children who had experienced a reliable adult waited around four times longer than those who had not. For a child who has learned that promises are often broken, or that food may be taken by others, eating the marshmallow immediately may be a perfectly rational choice.

Mischel himself, who died in 2018, always argued that self-control was not fixed and could be learned, and that the most important finding was not who waited, but how children managed to do so. Nevertheless, the revised findings suggest that teaching children individual strategies is unlikely, on its own, to have dramatic long-term effects. Improving the stability and resources of children's environments may matter just as much, if not more.

readingPassages.title: Is homework worth it?
paragraphs: Few aspects of school life cause as much argument as homework. For many parents, it is a sign that a school takes learning seriously; for others, it is a source of stress that takes away family time and leads to battles at the kitchen table. Teachers, too, are divided. Some see it as essential practice, while others regard it as a burden that widens the gap between children from different backgrounds. The research evidence, as is often the case in education, is more complicated than either side would like.

Homework has been controversial for more than a century. In the early twentieth century, some American doctors and journalists claimed that homework damaged children's health by depriving them of fresh air, exercise and sleep. In 1901, the state of California passed a law banning homework for children under the age of fifteen, although it was later repealed. Attitudes changed after 1957, when the Soviet Union launched the first satellite, Sputnik, and Americans worried that their children were falling behind. Homework was promoted as a way of raising standards, and the amount set increased.

The most widely cited research on the subject is by Harris Cooper of Duke University, who has reviewed hundreds of studies. His conclusion is that the effect of homework depends strongly on the age of the student. For secondary school students, there is a clear positive relationship between homework and achievement, up to a point. Beyond around two hours a night, however, the benefits disappear and may even reverse. For primary school children, Cooper found little evidence that homework improves academic achievement at all.

Why should age make such a difference? One explanation is that younger children are less able to study independently and to concentrate on tasks without help. They are also more easily distracted, and their parents may become heavily involved, sometimes in ways that are unhelpful. It is also possible that much of the homework given to young children is not well designed. Cooper himself does not recommend abolishing homework for primary pupils, however. He argues that short, simple tasks, such as reading for pleasure, can help children develop good study habits and show parents what their children are learning.

International comparisons add another dimension to the debate. Data from the OECD's PISA tests, which assess fifteen-year-olds around the world, show that students in countries such as Finland, which consistently perform well, do relatively little homework, whereas students in some lower-performing countries do a great deal. Yet within individual countries, students who do more homework tend to score higher. In my view, this suggests that the quality of teaching in school matters far more than the quantity of work done at home.

A particular concern is the effect of homework on inequality. Children from wealthier families are more likely to have a quiet place to study, access to a computer and the internet, and parents who have the time and education to help them. Children from poorer families may share a crowded room, have caring responsibilities or part-time jobs, or simply lack support. Homework may therefore reward advantages that have nothing to do with ability or effort. Some schools have responded by setting up homework clubs, where students can work after the school day with access to resources and staff.

There is also growing concern about the effect of homework on well-being. A study of students at high-achieving schools in California by Denise Pope of Stanford University found that many students did more than three hours of homework a night and reported high levels of stress, physical symptoms such as headaches and stomach problems, and a lack of balance in their lives. Pope does not argue that homework should be abolished, but she believes that much of it is set out of habit rather than for a clear purpose.

What, then, makes homework worthwhile? Most researchers agree that it should be purposeful, clearly linked to what is being taught in class, appropriate to the student's age and not excessive. Feedback matters too; homework that is never marked or discussed is unlikely to be taken seriously. Some schools have experimented with giving students choices about their homework, or with 'flipped learning', in which students watch short videos at home and then use class time for practice. These approaches deserve to be studied more carefully, but they suggest that the question is not simply whether to set homework, but how.
